da-2025-da-17.approach: Binary search needs two things: the data must be **sorted** (so one comparison can discard half), and the middle element must be reachable in **$O(1)$** (random access). Check each option against both requirements.

steps.title: What makes binary search $O(\log n)$
steps.body:
Each probe compares the key with the middle element $A[mid]$ and keeps only one half. The range shrinks $n \to n/2 \to n/4 \to \cdots \to 1$, i.e. at most $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ probes. This needs:

1. **Sorted order** — otherwise "key $<A[mid]$" says nothing about which half holds the key.
2. **$O(1)$ access to $A[mid]$** — otherwise each probe costs more than a constant.

scene.caption: Probe 1: compare with A[3] = 13; key 19 > 13, drop the left half

steps.title: Sorted array: every probe halves the range in $O(1)$
steps.body: In an array $A[mid]$ is one address computation away. With increasing order the halving works, so the worst case is $O(\log n)$ probes $\times\ O(1)$ each $= O(\log n)$. This is option (C).

scene.caption: Probe 2: A[5] = 21 > 19, keep A[4..4]; probe 3 finds 19 — 3 probes for n = 8

steps.title: Unsorted data fails the first requirement
steps.body: For "any order" (A, B) a comparison with the middle cannot rule out either half; the key may be anywhere, so the worst case needs to look at every element: $\Theta(n)$ (and binary search may even miss the key).

scene.label: B
scene.caption: Unsorted, key 21: probes 13 → 19 → 8 → 30 go right every time and miss 21 at index 0

steps.title: A linked list fails the second requirement
steps.body: In a linked list (D, even if sorted) reaching the middle node means following $n/2$ pointers. The probes walk $\frac{n}{2} + \frac{n}{4} + \cdots \approx n$ links, so the worst case is $\Theta(n)$ — the halving saves comparisons but not traversal time.

scene.label: list
scene.caption: Linked list: reaching the middle already costs 3 hops (n/2 in general)

answer.value: **An array of $n$ integers in increasing order** — option (C)

optionAnalysis.reason: Unsorted array: random access is fine, but without order a comparison cannot discard half of the array; finding a key needs $\Theta(n)$ in the worst case.
Unsorted **and** no random access — fails both requirements; $\Theta(n)$.
Sorted + $O(1)$ indexing: each probe halves the range, at most $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor + 1$ probes $\Rightarrow O(\log n)$.
Sorted, but reaching the middle of a linked list costs $\Theta(n)$ pointer hops; total traversal $\approx n/2 + n/4 + \cdots \approx n$, so $\Theta(n)$, not $O(\log n)$.

da-2025-da-17.shortcut: Binary search in O(log n) = sorted + random access. Only "array, increasing order" has both.
pitfalls: Picking (D) because the list is sorted — counting comparisons ($\log n$) but ignoring the $\Theta(n)$ pointer walking.
Thinking binary search "still works" on unsorted arrays — it can return "not found" for a present key.
da-2025-da-17.verification: Example: 8 sorted elements need at most $\lfloor \log_2 8\rfloor + 1 = 4$ probes; the same data in a linked list needs about 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 hops just to reach the probed nodes.

da-2025-da-18.approach: Find the eigenvalues of $A = I_n + xx^\top$ directly: $x$ itself is an eigenvector and every vector orthogonal to $x$ is another. All options then follow from the eigenvalues $\{2, 1, \ldots, 1\}$.

steps.title: $x$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $2$
steps.body: $$Ax = (I_n + xx^\top)x = x + x(x^\top x) = x + x \cdot 1 = 2x.$$

steps.title: Vectors orthogonal to $x$ have eigenvalue $1$
steps.body:
If $x^\top v = 0$ then $Av = v + x(x^\top v) = v + 0 = v$. The orthogonal complement of $x$ has dimension $n-1$, so eigenvalue $1$ has multiplicity $n - 1$.

Eigenvalues of $A$: $\{2, \underbrace{1, \ldots, 1}_{n-1}\}$, $\det A = 2 \cdot 1^{n-1} = 2$.

steps.title: Check the options
steps.body:
- No eigenvalue is $0$ $\Rightarrow$ $A$ is invertible and has full rank $n$ — (A) and (B) are true, (C) is false.
- $A^{-1}$ has eigenvalues $\frac{1}{2}$ and $1$ (reciprocals), all positive — (D) is false.

Explicitly, by Sherman–Morrison, $A^{-1} = I_n - \frac{1}{2}xx^\top$ (check: $(I + xx^\top)(I - \tfrac12 xx^\top) = I + xx^\top - \tfrac12 xx^\top - \tfrac12 x(x^\top x)x^\top = I$).

optionAnalysis.reason: All eigenvalues ($2$ and $1$) are non-zero and $A$ is symmetric, so rank $= n$.
$\det A = 2 \ne 0$; indeed $A^{-1} = I_n - \tfrac12 xx^\top$.
Eigenvalues are only $2$ and $1$. Confusing $I + xx^\top$ with $I - xx^\top$ (a projection, which does have eigenvalue $0$ along $x$) gives this distractor.
$A^{-1}$ has eigenvalues $\tfrac12$ and $1$ — both positive ($A$ is positive definite, so is $A^{-1}$).

da-2025-da-18.shortcut: Eigenvalues of $I + uu^\top$ are $1 + \lVert u\rVert^2$ (once) and $1$ ($n-1$ times). With $\lVert x \rVert = 1$: $\{2, 1, \ldots, 1\}$.
pitfalls: Thinking $xx^\top$ has rank 1 so $A$ is "rank-deficient" — adding $I_n$ makes it full rank.
Mixing up $I + xx^\top$ with the projection $I - xx^\top$.
da-2025-da-18.verification: Take $n = 2$, $x = (1, 0)^\top$: $A = \mathrm{diag}(2, 1)$, rank 2, invertible, eigenvalues 2 and 1, $A^{-1} = \mathrm{diag}(\tfrac12, 1)$ — matches (A), (B) and rules out (C), (D).

da-2025-da-19.approach: The number of swaps made by insertion sort equals the number of **inversions** (pairs $i<j$ with $a_i > a_j$). The fixed part already has one inversion, $(15, 13)$, so $x$ must create **exactly one** more.
da-2025-da-19.given: Array $[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, x, 15, 13]$; insertion sort makes exactly $2$ swaps.

steps.title: Swaps = inversions
steps.body:
Insertion sort moves each element left by swapping it with every larger element before it, and each swap removes exactly one inversion. So #swaps $=$ #inversions.

Without $x$: $1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 13$ has exactly one inversion, $(15, 13)$. Hence $x$ must be in exactly **one** inversion.

steps.title: Inversions involving $x$
steps.body:
$x$ forms an inversion with every element **before** it that is larger ($1,\ldots,11$) and every element **after** it that is smaller ($15, 13$):

| $x$ | larger before | smaller after | inversions with $x$ | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 11 | — | 1 | **2** |
| 12 | — | — | 0 | 1 |
| 14 | — | 13 | 1 | **2** |
| 16 | — | 15, 13 | 2 | 3 |

steps.title: $x = 10$: one extra swap (with 11)
steps.body: Inserting $10$ swaps it once past $11$; later $13$ swaps once past $15$. Total $1 + 1 = 2$ swaps. ✓

steps.title: $x = 14$: one extra swap (13 passes 14)
steps.body: $14$ stays in place when inserted; when $13$ is inserted it swaps past $15$ and then past $14$: $2$ swaps in total. ✓

steps.title: $x = 12$ and $x = 16$ fail
steps.body: $x = 12$ sits between $11$ and $15$ and is smaller than $13$ — no inversion, only $1$ swap. $x = 16$ is larger than both $15$ and $13$ after it — $2$ inversions, $3$ swaps.

optionAnalysis.reason: Inversions $(11, 10)$ and $(15, 13)$: exactly 2 swaps.
$11 < 12 < 13 < 15$, so $12$ adds no inversion; only the swap $(15, 13)$ — 1 swap.
Inversions $(14, 13)$ and $(15, 13)$: exactly 2 swaps.
$16$ is larger than both $15$ and $13$ after it: inversions $(16, 15), (16, 13), (15, 13)$ — 3 swaps.

da-2025-da-19.shortcut: Need $x$ in exactly one inversion: either $9 < x < 11$ (one larger element before it) or $13 < x < 15$ (one smaller element after it). Only 10 and 14 qualify.
pitfalls: Forgetting the built-in inversion $(15, 13)$ and looking for $x$ with two inversions (would give 16).
Counting comparisons instead of swaps.
da-2025-da-19.verification: Simulating insertion sort on $[\ldots, 11, 14, 15, 13]$: 14 stays; 15 stays; 13 swaps with 15, then with 14, then stops at 11 — 2 swaps. For $x = 10$: 10 swaps with 11 (stops at 9); 15 stays; 13 swaps with 15 — 2 swaps.

da-2025-da-20.approach: Recall the definitions: **single** linkage measures the distance between the two **closest** members of the clusters (min), **complete** linkage between the two **farthest** members (max).

steps.title: Single linkage = nearest pair = DIS-2
steps.body:
Single-linkage (nearest-neighbour) clustering defines
$$d_{\text{single}}(C_1, C_2) = \min_{x \in C_1,\, y \in C_2} D(x, y),$$
which is **DIS-2**. It merges clusters if *any* two members are close, so it tends to form long chains.

scene.caption: Closest cross pair a3–b1 → single linkage (DIS-2)

steps.title: Complete linkage = farthest pair = DIS-1
steps.body:
Complete-linkage (farthest-neighbour) clustering defines
$$d_{\text{complete}}(C_1, C_2) = \max_{x \in C_1,\, y \in C_2} D(x, y),$$
which is **DIS-1**. Two clusters are close only if *all* their members are close, giving compact clusters.

scene.caption: Farthest cross pair a1–b3 → complete linkage (DIS-1)

steps.title: Match with the options
steps.body:
| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| (A) Single uses DIS-1 (max) | false — single uses min |
| (B) Single uses DIS-2 (min) | **true** |
| (C) Complete uses DIS-2 (min) | false — complete uses max |
| (D) Complete uses DIS-1 (max) | **true** |

answer.value: Options **(B)** and **(D)**: single linkage uses DIS-2 (min), complete linkage uses DIS-1 (max)

optionAnalysis.reason: DIS-1 is the **maximum** pairwise distance — that is complete linkage, not single.
Single linkage uses the minimum pairwise distance $= $ DIS-2.
DIS-2 (minimum) is single linkage; complete linkage uses the maximum.
Complete linkage uses the maximum pairwise distance $=$ DIS-1.

da-2025-da-20.shortcut: "Single" = one closest link suffices (min); "complete" = every pair must be close, so the worst pair counts (max).
pitfalls: Swapping the two: the word "complete" refers to all pairs being within the distance, which is governed by the maximum.
da-2025-da-20.verification: Average linkage (mean of all $D(x,y)$) always lies between DIS-2 and DIS-1, consistent with single ≤ average ≤ complete.

da-2025-da-21.approach: Bayes' theorem: $P(\text{Box-2} \mid W) = \dfrac{P(\text{Box-2})\,P(W \mid \text{Box-2})}{\sum_i P(\text{Box-}i)\,P(W \mid \text{Box-}i)}$. Working in eighteenths keeps all fractions integer.

steps.title: Joint probability of each box and a white ball
steps.body:
- Box-1: $\frac12 \times \frac13 = \frac16 = \frac{3}{18}$
- Box-2: $\frac16 \times \frac23 = \frac{2}{18}$
- Box-3: $\frac13 \times \frac12 = \frac16 = \frac{3}{18}$

scene.caption: Box-2 branch: 2 of the 8 white-weight units

da-2025-da-21.shortcut: Scale priors to 9/18, 3/18, 6/18 → "white weights" 9·⅓ = 3, 3·⅔ = 2, 6·½ = 3 → Box-2 share 2/8 = 0.25.
pitfalls: Ignoring the unequal priors and answering $\frac{2/3}{1/3 + 2/3 + 1/2} = 0.4$.
Using $P(W \mid \text{Box-2}) = \frac23$ itself as the answer.
da-2025-da-21.verification: Posteriors of all boxes: $\frac38, \frac28, \frac38$ — they sum to $1$.

da-2025-da-22.approach: An $\infty - \infty$ form with a square root: multiply and divide by the conjugate $\sqrt{t^2+t} + t$, then divide numerator and denominator by $t$.

steps.title: Identify the indeterminate form
steps.body: As $t \to +\infty$ both $\sqrt{t^2+t}$ and $t$ tend to $\infty$, so the expression is of the form $\infty - \infty$ and cannot be evaluated by substitution. A difference involving a square root is resolved by multiplying by the conjugate.

steps.title: Rationalise
steps.body: $$\sqrt{t^2+t} - t = \frac{(\sqrt{t^2+t} - t)(\sqrt{t^2+t} + t)}{\sqrt{t^2+t} + t} = \frac{(t^2 + t) - t^2}{\sqrt{t^2+t} + t} = \frac{t}{\sqrt{t^2+t} + t}.$$

steps.title: Divide by $t$ and let $t \to +\infty$
steps.body:
For $t > 0$, $\sqrt{t^2 + t} = t\sqrt{1 + \frac1t}$, so
$$\frac{t}{t\sqrt{1 + \frac1t} + t} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \frac1t} + 1} \;\xrightarrow{t \to \infty}\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{1} + 1} = \frac12 = 0.5.$$

da-2025-da-22.shortcut: Binomial expansion: $\sqrt{t^2 + t} = t\left(1 + \frac1t\right)^{1/2} = t\left(1 + \frac{1}{2t} - \frac{1}{8t^2} + \cdots\right) = t + \frac12 - \frac{1}{8t} + \cdots$, so the difference tends to $\frac12$.
pitfalls: Writing $\sqrt{t^2 + t} \approx t$ and concluding the limit is $0$ — the lower-order term contributes $\frac12$.
Answering $\infty - \infty = 0$ without resolving the indeterminate form.

da-2025-da-23.approach: The subquery is **uncorrelated**, so evaluate it once to a single number, then filter the outer table with that constant.

steps.title: Read the query
steps.body: The inner query does not refer to \`L1\`, so it is an **uncorrelated scalar subquery**: it returns one value (the largest SR Nagar loan) and the outer query keeps every loan whose amount is **strictly greater** than that value. Each qualifying loan gives one row.

steps.title: Filter: amount > 65000
steps.body:
Compare every loan with $65000$ (strictly greater):

- L11: $90000 > 65000$ ✓
- L23: $80000 > 65000$ ✓
- L25: $70000 > 65000$ ✓
- L19: $65000 > 65000$? No (equal). L14, L15, L22 are smaller.

Rows returned: L11, L23, L25 $\Rightarrow$ **3**.

pitfalls: Using $\ge$ and also counting L19 (65000), giving 4.
Taking the overall MAX (90000) instead of the SR Nagar MAX, giving 0.

da-2025-da-24.approach: For the no-intercept model $y = wx$, minimise $L(w) = \sum_i (y_i - w x_i)^2$; setting $L'(w) = 0$ gives the closed form $w^* = \dfrac{\sum x_i y_i}{\sum x_i^2}$.

steps.title: Normal equation
steps.body:
$$L(w) = \sum_{i}(y_i - w x_i)^2,\qquad L'(w) = -2\sum_i x_i (y_i - w x_i) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; w^* = \frac{\sum_i x_i y_i}{\sum_i x_i^2}.$$
$L''(w) = 2\sum x_i^2 > 0$, so this is the minimum.

pitfalls: Dropping the minus signs (data read as (1,1), (2,5), (3,5) gives $26/14 \approx 1.857$).
Using the slope formula with an intercept, $\frac{\mathrm{cov}(x,y)}{\mathrm{var}(x)}$, which fits a different model.

da-2025-da-25.approach: The (naive) Bayes classifier picks the class with the larger posterior; it errs exactly when the true class is the other one, so $P(\text{error} \mid x) = \min\big(P(y_1 \mid x), P(y_2 \mid x)\big)$.

steps.title: Joint probabilities
steps.body: $$P(y_1)P(x\mid y_1) = \frac13 \cdot \frac34 = \frac14 = \frac{3}{12},\qquad P(y_2)P(x\mid y_2) = \frac23 \cdot \frac14 = \frac16 = \frac{2}{12}.$$

steps.title: Posteriors and decision
steps.body:
$$P(x) = \frac{3}{12} + \frac{2}{12} = \frac{5}{12},\quad P(y_1\mid x) = \frac{3/12}{5/12} = \frac35 = 0.6,\quad P(y_2\mid x) = \frac25 = 0.4.$$
The classifier assigns $x$ to $y_1$ (larger posterior).

scene.caption: Predict y₁; wrong whenever the true class is y₂

steps.title: Probability of misclassification
steps.body:
Predicting $y_1$ is wrong exactly when the true class is $y_2$:
$$P(\text{error} \mid x) = P(y_2 \mid x) = \frac25 = 0.40.$$

da-2025-da-25.shortcut: Compare $1 \cdot 3 = 3$ with $2 \cdot 1 = 2$ (priors × likelihoods, common denominators dropped): error $= \frac{2}{3+2} = 0.4$.
pitfalls: Answering $0.6$ (probability of the chosen class).
Picking $y_2$ because its prior is larger — the likelihood ratio 3:1 outweighs the prior ratio 1:2.
Reporting the unnormalised $\frac16 \approx 0.17$.

da-2025-da-26.approach: $Z$ is standard normal, so $Y = Z^2 \sim \chi^2_1$. Use $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = E[Z^4] - (E[Z^2])^2$ with the normal moments $E[Z^2] = 1$, $E[Z^4] = 3$.

steps.title: $Z$ is standard normal
steps.body: $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2) \Rightarrow Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim N(0, 1)$, so $E[Z^2] = \mathrm{Var}(Z) + (E[Z])^2 = 1 + 0 = 1$.

steps.title: Fourth moment
steps.body:
For $N(0,1)$, $E[Z^{2k}] = (2k-1)!! $, so $E[Z^4] = 3 \cdot 1 = 3$.

(By parts: $E[Z^4] = \int z^3 \cdot z\,\phi(z)\,dz = 3\int z^2 \phi(z)\,dz = 3E[Z^2] = 3$, using $z\phi(z) = -\phi'(z)$.)

optionAnalysis.reason: $1$ is $E[Y] = E[Z^2]$ (or $\mathrm{Var}(Z)$), not the variance of $Y$.
$E[Z^4] - (E[Z^2])^2 = 3 - 1 = 2$; equivalently $\chi^2_k$ has variance $2k$ with $k = 1$.
$3$ is $E[Z^4] = E[Y^2]$ — forgetting to subtract $(E[Y])^2 = 1$.
$4$ is the variance of $\chi^2_2$ (a sum of **two** squared standard normals); here only one normal is squared.

da-2025-da-26.shortcut: $Y = Z^2 \sim \chi^2_1$; a $\chi^2_k$ variable has mean $k$ and variance $2k$ → $2$.
pitfalls: Answering $3$ ($= E[Z^4]$) by forgetting to subtract the squared mean.
Thinking the answer depends on $\mu$ or $\sigma$ — standardisation removes them.

da-2025-da-27.approach: Test options with simple matrices satisfying $A^3 = A$ ($0$, $I$, $\mathrm{diag}(1,0)$) to kill (A)–(C); prove (D) with the rank inequality $\operatorname{rank}(PQ) \le \min(\operatorname{rank} P, \operatorname{rank} Q)$ applied both ways.

steps.title: Counterexamples for (A), (B), (C)
steps.body:
- $A = 0$: $0^3 = 0$, but $0$ is not invertible ⇒ (A) not always true.
- $A = I_n$: $I^3 = I$, $\det I = 1 \ne 0$ ⇒ (B) not always true; trace $= n$, which is $\ne 1$ for $n \ge 2$ (and $A = 0$ has trace $0$) ⇒ (C) not always true.

steps.title: (D): $\operatorname{rank}(A^2) \le \operatorname{rank}(A)$
steps.body: $A^2 = A \cdot A$, and the rank of a product never exceeds the rank of a factor, so $\operatorname{rank}(A^2) \le \operatorname{rank}(A)$.

steps.title: (D): $\operatorname{rank}(A) \le \operatorname{rank}(A^2)$
steps.body:
Using $A^3 = A$: $A = A^2 \cdot A$, so $\operatorname{rank}(A) = \operatorname{rank}(A^2 A) \le \operatorname{rank}(A^2)$.

Both inequalities ⇒ $\operatorname{rank}(A) = \operatorname{rank}(A^2)$ for **every** such $A$.

scene.caption: rank A = rank A² in every row

answer.value: **$A$ and $A^2$ have the same rank** — option (D)

optionAnalysis.reason: $A = 0$ satisfies $A^3 = A$ and is singular.
$A = I_n$ satisfies $A^3 = A$ with $\det A = 1$.
$A = I_n$ has trace $n$ and $A = 0$ has trace $0$; the trace of such an $A$ is (number of $+1$ eigenvalues) $-$ (number of $-1$ eigenvalues), not fixed at $1$.
$\operatorname{rank}(A^2) \le \operatorname{rank}(A)$ and $\operatorname{rank}(A) = \operatorname{rank}(A^2 \cdot A) \le \operatorname{rank}(A^2)$.

da-2025-da-27.shortcut: $x^3 - x = x(x-1)(x+1)$ has distinct roots, so $A$ is diagonalisable with eigenvalues in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$; $A^2$ has the same zero eigenvalues ⇒ same rank.
pitfalls: Cancelling $A$ in $A^3 = A$ to get $A^2 = I$ — only valid if $A$ is invertible.
Concluding $\det A = 0$ from $\det(A)^3 = \det(A)$, which also allows $\det A = \pm 1$.
da-2025-da-27.verification: Diagonalisable view: $A = PDP^{-1}$, $D = \mathrm{diag}(d_i)$, $d_i \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$; $A^2 = PD^2P^{-1}$ with $d_i^2 = 0 \iff d_i = 0$, so both have rank $= \#\{d_i \ne 0\}$.

da-2025-da-28.approach: $A$ is the **Gram matrix** $A = X^\top X$ where $X = [x_1 \;\cdots\; x_n]$ has the given vectors as columns. Independence makes $X$ invertible, so $A$ is invertible (indeed positive definite).

steps.title: Write $A$ as $X^\top X$
steps.body: Let $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ have columns $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. Then $(X^\top X)_{ij} = x_i^\top x_j = A_{ij}$, so $A = X^\top X$.

steps.title: $X$ is invertible
steps.body: The $n$ columns of $X$ are linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$, so $X$ has rank $n$ and $\det X \ne 0$.

steps.title: $A$ is invertible and positive definite
steps.body:
$$\det A = \det(X^\top)\det(X) = (\det X)^2 > 0.$$
Also, for $z \ne 0$: $z^\top A z = z^\top X^\top X z = \lVert Xz \rVert^2 > 0$ because $Xz \ne 0$ (independent columns). So $A$ is positive definite: all eigenvalues and singular values are $> 0$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\det A = (\det X)^2 > 0$.
$A$ is symmetric positive definite, so its singular values equal its eigenvalues, all $> 0$; $0$ is not one of them.
$\det A = (\det X)^2 \ne 0$. It would be $0$ only if the vectors were dependent.
$z^\top A z = \lVert Xz\rVert^2 = 0$ forces $Xz = 0$, i.e. $z = 0$, since the columns are independent.

da-2025-da-28.shortcut: Gram matrix of linearly independent vectors = positive definite ⇒ invertible. (B), (C), (D) all say "singular / not PD" in disguise.
pitfalls: Thinking $A = XX^\top$ instead of $X^\top X$ — here both are invertible anyway, but the identification matters for non-square $X$.

da-2025-da-29.approach: Convert the event on $X^2$ to an interval on $X$: $X^2 \le 0.25 \iff -0.5 \le X \le 0.5$. The CDF is continuous, so the probability is $F_X(0.5) - F_X(-0.5)$.
concepts: CDF of a continuous random variable

steps.title: Turn the event into an interval
steps.body:
$$X^2 \le 0.25 \iff \lvert X \rvert \le 0.5 \iff -0.5 \le X \le 0.5.$$
$F_X$ is continuous (it equals $0$ at $x = -1$ and $1$ at $x = 1$ from both formulas), so $P(X = -0.5) = 0$ and
$$P(-0.5 \le X \le 0.5) = F_X(0.5) - F_X(-0.5).$$

optionAnalysis.reason: $0.625$ comes from wrong arithmetic such as $F(0.5) + F(-0.5)$ $= 0.5625 + 0.0625$.
$0.25 = F_X(0) = P(X \le 0)$ (or just the threshold $0.25$ itself) — not the probability of $\lvert X\rvert \le 0.5$.
$0.5625 = F_X(0.5) = P(X \le 0.5)$ — forgetting the lower bound $X \ge -0.5$.

da-2025-da-29.shortcut: Density $f(x) = \frac{x+1}{2}$ on $[-1,1]$; over the symmetric interval $[-0.5, 0.5]$ the odd part $\frac x2$ integrates to 0, leaving $\frac12 \times 1 = 0.5$.
pitfalls: Answering $P(X \le 0.5) = 0.5625$ by ignoring the negative side.
Using $P(X \le 0.25)$ — the event is on $X^2$, not $X$.
